why.correct: The perimysium wraps each fascicle, a bundle of muscle fibers. The larger blood vessels and nerves run into the muscle along it.

The perimysium surrounds a whole fascicle, not one fiber.

Actin forms the two twisted strands of beads that the rod lies along.
Myosin makes up the thick filament, not the thin one.

why.correct: A muscle is a bundle of fascicles; a fascicle is a bundle of fibers (cells); each fiber is packed with myofibrils; each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres; and each sarcomere is built from thick and thin filaments.

Correct. The I band contains thin filaments only.

why.correct: A sarcomere runs from one Z disc to the next. The Z discs anchor the thin filaments.

The H zone is the paler middle of the A band, at the sarcomere's center.

Triads are membrane structures (a T tubule and two terminal cisternae) near the A band edges. They do not define the sarcomere.

why.correct: A thin filament is two twisted strands of actin, with tropomyosin lying in the groove and troponin attached to the tropomyosin at intervals.
options: Correct. Actin forms the backbone of the thin filament.
Myosin forms the thick filament, and its heads reach toward the thin filament.
Correct. Troponin is the small complex on tropomyosin that can bind calcium.
Correct. Tropomyosin is the rod that covers the myosin-binding sites at rest.

The perimysium surrounds groups of fibers (fascicles), not each fiber.
Deep fascia lies outside whole muscles.

why.correct: A T tubule is an infolding of the sarcolemma, so its inside is open to the extracellular fluid. The dye flows into the T tubules without crossing any membrane.

Correct. The T tubules are continuous with the fluid outside the cell.
The myofibrils lie in the sarcoplasm, inside the sarcolemma, which the dye cannot cross.
The sarcoplasm is the cytoplasm, inside the cell membrane.

Myofibrils are not grouped in threes; a triad is a membrane structure.
Each thick filament is surrounded by six thin filaments, and filaments are not what the word triad names.
A Z disc with half an I band on each side describes the region around a sarcomere boundary, not a triad.

why.correct: T tubules are infoldings of the sarcolemma that reach every myofibril. The electrical signal travels down them to the triads throughout the fiber, where the SR beside each myofibril holds the calcium.
options: Calcium diffusing inward from the surface would reach the center far too slowly; the calcium used comes from the SR inside the fiber.
Myofibrils are not cells, so there are no gap junctions between them.

A skeletal muscle fiber's nuclei lie at its edge, just under the sarcolemma, and they do not relay signals.

why.correct: The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of the whole fiber, the cell. Myofibrils are structures inside the cell, with no membrane of their own; the SR network wraps around them.

options: Correct. Tropomyosin blocks the binding sites while calcium is low.
The filaments do overlap at rest, throughout the A band outside the H zone.
The heads carry the products of split ATP at rest; lack of ATP is not what holds them off.
Titin centers the thick filament and gives elasticity; it does not restrain the heads.

Correct. The A band spans the thick filaments.
The Z disc is a thin line at each end of the sarcomere, anchoring thin filaments.
The M line is a thin line at the center of the A band, not the whole dark band.

why.correct: Convert to the same unit: 3 cm = 30,000 µm. Then divide: 30,000 µm ÷ 2.5 µm = 12,000 sarcomeres.

why.correct: Each myofibril has alternating dark A bands and light I bands, and neighboring myofibrils keep their bands in step. Lined up across the fiber, they form continuous stripes.
options: The nuclei are scattered along the edge of the fiber, not arranged in rows that make stripes.
The SR wraps every myofibril as a lacy network; the stripes come from the filaments, not the SR.

The endomysium lies outside the fiber and has no banded pattern.

why.correct: The three connective tissue layers are continuous with each other and merge into the tendon's collagen. Each fiber's pull passes outward through them, so a hard sprint concentrates force where muscle meets tendon.

Myofibrils stay inside their fibers; they end at the fiber's ends, where proteins link them to the sarcolemma and the connective tissue outside.
Deep fascia groups whole muscles; the pull reaches the tendon through the muscle's own wrappings.

why.correct: The nerve impulse opens calcium channels; calcium triggers exocytosis of acetylcholine; acetylcholine crosses the cleft and opens ligand-gated channels on the end plate; the resulting end plate potential brings the nearby membrane to threshold, and the muscle fiber fires an action potential.
The pinned protein sits in the folded membrane of the motor end plate. It is a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor protein, a ligand-gated channel that lets sodium in when acetylcholine binds.
options: Correct. It is the ACh receptor protein, a channel in the end plate.
Synaptic vesicles are the round sacs inside the axon terminal, not proteins in the muscle membrane.
Voltage-gated calcium channels are in the axon terminal's membrane, not in the end plate.
AChE is an enzyme anchored in the cleft; it is not a channel through the end plate membrane.

variables.name: Action potentials reaching the axon terminal

variables.name: Acetylcholine released per nerve impulse

variables.name: Size of the end plate potential

variables.name: Action potentials in the muscle fibers

why.correct: Acetylcholinesterase ends each signal by splitting acetylcholine. Slowing it leaves acetylcholine in the cleft longer, so each release opens channels for longer and the end plate stays depolarized longer. Release itself is unchanged.

variables.name: Acetylcholine released by the terminal
variables.why: Release depends on calcium entry into the terminal, which the drug does not change.

variables.name: Time acetylcholine stays in the synaptic cleft

variables.name: Duration of the end plate potential
variables.why: Lingering acetylcholine keeps binding receptor proteins and reopening their channels, so the depolarization lasts longer.

variables.name: Choline returned to the axon terminal per second
variables.why: Choline comes from splitting acetylcholine; slower splitting produces choline more slowly.

why.correct: Release is calcium-triggered. The action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the calcium that flows in makes the vesicles fuse. With no calcium outside, nothing flows in and no acetylcholine is released.
options: The fibers' sodium channels do not need outside calcium to open; the chain fails earlier, at release from the terminal.
The question says the action potentials do reach and depolarize the terminals; it is the next step that fails.
Correct. No calcium entry means no exocytosis of acetylcholine.
If the enzyme failed, acetylcholine would linger and the muscle would respond more, not less.

why.correct: Botulinum toxin destroys proteins the vesicles need to fuse with the terminal membrane. Calcium enters normally, but acetylcholine stays inside the terminal, so the muscle gets no signal.
options: Calcium channels open normally in botulism; the failure comes one step later, at fusion.
Correct. Without vesicle fusion, no acetylcholine is released.
Blocking the receptor proteins is how curare-type drugs work; the toxin acts inside the terminal.
Blocking breakdown would make acetylcholine linger and cause quivering, not a failure of release.

why.correct: In trace B the membrane depolarizes only to about −75 mV and fades, well below the threshold line at about −55 mV. With most receptor proteins blocked, too few channels open, and a graded potential that does not reach threshold triggers nothing.
options: The threshold line is the same for both traces; what changed is how far the membrane depolarized.
Trace B still shows a small depolarization, so some acetylcholine was released and bound. With no release at all there would be no bump.
Correct. The end plate potential stayed below threshold.
Trace B returns to rest within a few milliseconds; it does not stay depolarized.

why.correct: Rocuronium blocks the receptor proteins competitively. Slowing acetylcholinesterase lets acetylcholine accumulate in the cleft, and at higher concentration it wins more binding sites, opens more channels and brings the end plate potential back above threshold.
options: Neostigmine inhibits the enzyme that splits acetylcholine; it does not break down rocuronium.
Neostigmine acts at the junction, not on how often the motor neuron fires.
The threshold of the sarcolemma is unchanged; the end plate potential grows back to reach it.
Correct. More acetylcholine competes the blocker off the receptor proteins.

why.correct: The end plate potential is a graded, local depolarization made by acetylcholine opening ligand-gated channels. In a healthy junction it is large enough to bring the neighboring membrane to threshold with room to spare. The action potential it triggers is what is all-or-none and travels the whole fiber.
options: Correct. More acetylcholine and more open channels make a bigger end plate potential.
It is graded; the action potential it triggers is all-or-none.
Correct. Acetylcholine opens the nicotinic receptor channels.
It fades within a short distance; the action potential carries the signal along the fiber.
Correct. This safety margin makes transmission reliable.

why.correct: Acetylcholine is built from an acetyl group and choline. The enzyme splits it back into acetate and choline, and a transport protein returns the choline to the terminal.
options: Correct. Choline is recycled into new acetylcholine.
Calcium triggers release; it is not a product of splitting acetylcholine.
The products are acetate and choline; no phosphate is involved.
Glucose is a fuel, not part of acetylcholine.

why.correct: At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholinesterase in the cleft ends the signal by splitting acetylcholine into acetate and choline. Only the choline is taken back into the terminal.
options: This step is right. Depolarization of the terminal opens its calcium channels.
This step is right. Calcium entry makes the vesicles fuse and release acetylcholine.
This step is right. The receptor protein is a ligand-gated channel, and sodium's inward push dominates.
This step is right. The end plate potential brings the nearby membrane, rich in voltage-gated sodium channels, to threshold.
This is the error. Acetylcholine is split in the cleft, not taken back intact.

why.correct: At −90 mV, sodium is pulled in by both its concentration gradient and the negative inside, so its inward push is large. Potassium is near its equilibrium potential, about −90 mV, so its outward push is small. More positive charge enters than leaves.
options: Potassium can pass, but at −90 mV it is close to its equilibrium potential, so little leaves.
Correct. The electrochemical gradient for sodium dominates.
Acetylcholine binds the outside of the channel and is not carried across the membrane.
A channel allows passive flow down gradients; it does not pump.

why.correct: A normal end plate potential is about three to five times larger than needed to reach threshold. Halving the receptor proteins shrinks it, but it can still reach threshold, so every fiber still fires. Weakness appears only when the end plate potential falls below threshold, often first during repeated firing.
options: Correct. The safety margin absorbs the loss.
Skeletal muscle fibers are excited only through their neuromuscular junctions; no calcium-based excitation takes over.
Release depends on calcium entry into the terminal, which the toxin does not change.
An action potential in a fiber is all-or-none, and each fiber's response does not double to cover for another.

why.correct: With the enzyme blocked, acetylcholine lingers and keeps the end plate depolarized. Early on, the prolonged end plate potential fires repeated action potentials, so muscles quiver. With lasting depolarization, voltage-gated sodium channels around the end plate close and stay closed, so the fiber can no longer fire.
options: The terminals still make and release acetylcholine; the problem is that it is not cleared.
Acetylcholine binds and releases its receptor proteins without destroying them.
Correct. A persistently depolarized membrane cannot fire new action potentials.
Organophosphates block acetylcholinesterase, not calcium channels.

why.correct: Acetylcholinesterase is anchored in the basal lamina of the synaptic cleft, where it splits acetylcholine as soon as it is released.
options: The vesicles hold acetylcholine; the enzyme that splits it would destroy it there.
The SR stores calcium inside the muscle fiber and plays no part in clearing acetylcholine.
Correct. The enzyme sits in the cleft, between terminal and end plate.
Acetylcholine is made in the terminal's cytosol; the enzyme that splits it acts outside, in the cleft.

why.correct: Transmission at the neuromuscular junction is one for one. Each impulse releases enough acetylcholine to bring every fiber the neuron supplies to threshold, and each fires one action potential.
options: Correct. The large end plate potential guarantees one muscle action potential per nerve impulse.
Each fiber has one junction from one motor neuron, and that single input is enough; no adding up of inputs is needed.
That describes most single inputs between neurons in the brain, not the neuromuscular junction.
Every branch of the axon ends on its own fiber and releases acetylcholine there.

why.correct: A motor neuron is the efferent pathway to an effector. Those that supply skeletal muscle have cell bodies in the spinal cord or brain and long axons that end at neuromuscular junctions.
options: Carrying information in from the skin is an afferent job, the opposite direction.
Correct. Motor neurons carry commands out to effectors such as skeletal muscle fibers.
Glial cells insulate axons, but they are not neurons.
Skeletal muscle fibers do not set their own rhythm; they fire only when a motor neuron signals.

why.correct: Rocuronium occupies the acetylcholine binding sites on the nicotinic receptor proteins without opening them. Acetylcholine is released but cannot open enough channels, so the end plate potential stays below threshold.
options: Calcium entry must be normal, because the terminals are releasing normal amounts of acetylcholine.
The question states that release is normal.
Correct. The receptor proteins are blocked.
The fibers never fire an action potential, so the problem is upstream of anything inside them.

why.correct: The action potential spreads over the fiber and into the T tubules. At the triads, the voltage-sensing DHP receptors pull open the ryanodine receptors, calcium leaves the SR, binds troponin, and tropomyosin moves off the binding sites so myosin can bind actin.

Relaxation runs the chain backward: no release, the cleft is cleared, the membrane rests so the release channels close, ATP-driven pumps return calcium to the SR, calcium leaves troponin, and tropomyosin blocks actin again.

Calcium stays bound to troponin until the SR pumps bring the sarcoplasmic calcium back down, which takes tens of milliseconds. Force builds while calcium is present, even though the release channels closed when the action potential ended.
options: The top trace shows a single action potential; nothing else fires.
Correct. The calcium trace falls slowly because pumping back takes time.
Acetylcholinesterase clears acetylcholine within a millisecond or two.
The release channels close when the membrane repolarizes; the calcium trace starts falling within 10 ms.

why.correct: Calcium ATPases in the SR membrane pump calcium from the sarcoplasm back into the SR, two ions per ATP, against a steep gradient. As they do, calcium leaves troponin and force falls.
options: A little calcium does leave across the sarcolemma, but most returns to the SR, and it moves against its gradient, so it is pumped, not diffused.
Calcium is an ion; it is moved, not broken down.
Correct. SR calcium pumps clear the sarcoplasm by primary active transport.
Calcium binds troponin on the thin filaments, and only while its concentration is high.

why.correct: The DHP receptor is the voltage sensor. When the T tubule depolarizes it changes shape, and because it is linked to the ryanodine receptor, it pulls that release channel open.
options: Pumping calcium back is the job of the SR calcium ATPase.
Correct. It is the voltage sensor linked to the release channel.
Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptor proteins on the motor end plate, not in the T tubules.
In skeletal muscle, the calcium that binds troponin comes from the SR, not from outside; the DHP receptor's job is to sense voltage.

why.correct: Dantrolene cuts the chain after the electrical steps. The fiber is excited normally, but the SR does not release its calcium, so the troponin switch stays mostly off and force falls. This is how it stops the runaway calcium leak of a faulty release channel.

variables.name: End plate potential
variables.why: Acetylcholine release and its receptor proteins are unaffected, so the end plate depolarizes as before.

variables.name: Action potentials in the sarcolemma and T tubules

variables.name: Calcium in the sarcoplasm after each action potential
variables.why: With the release channels blocked, the DHP receptors cannot open them, so little calcium leaves the SR.

variables.name: Force of contraction
variables.why: Less calcium binds troponin, so fewer binding sites on actin are uncovered and fewer myosin heads can pull.

why.correct: The SR calcium pumps end contraction by clearing calcium. Blocking them leaves release unchanged but makes calcium, and therefore contraction, last much longer, and it empties the store.

variables.name: Calcium released from the SR by this action potential
variables.why: Release through the ryanodine receptors does not depend on the pumps, so this first release is normal.

variables.why: The pumps are what remove calcium from the sarcoplasm; without them it lingers.

why.correct: Skeletal muscle takes the calcium for contraction from its SR, so low blood calcium does not starve the filaments. Instead, low extracellular calcium lets voltage-gated sodium channels open closer to the resting potential. Nerves and fibers fire without a command, and muscles spasm.
options: The filaments' calcium comes from the SR regardless of blood calcium; the spasms come from excess firing.
The SR pumps keep working; the problem is extra action potentials, not failed relaxation.
Opening of the release channels depends on the DHP receptors sensing voltage, not on blood calcium.
Correct. Hyperexcitable membranes fire spontaneously, causing spasms.

why.correct: Direct stimulation bypasses the neuromuscular junction, whose transmitter release does need outside calcium. The fiber's action potential then opens the SR release channels through the linked DHP receptors, so contraction uses calcium stored inside the fiber.
options: Correct. Voltage opens the SR store; outside calcium is not needed.
Calcium is still the switch; it simply comes from inside the fiber.
An electrode delivers current, not calcium ions.
Troponin must bind calcium before tropomyosin moves; the calcium comes from the SR.

why.correct: Calcium binds troponin, not tropomyosin. Troponin then changes shape and lets tropomyosin roll off the binding sites.
options: This step is right. T tubule membrane is sarcolemma and carries the action potential inward.
This step is right. The DHP receptor is the voltage sensor.
This step is right. The release channels open and calcium flows out down its gradient.
This is the error. Troponin is the calcium-binding protein.
This step is right. Once uncovered, the binding sites are available to the energized heads.

why.correct: Troponin is the calcium-binding complex on the thin filament. Calcium binding changes its shape, and it releases tropomyosin from its blocking position.
options: Correct. Troponin is the calcium sensor of the thin filament.
Myosin binds actin and ATP; the switch that calcium flips is on the thin filament.
Titin is an elastic protein running from the Z disc to the M line; it is not the calcium switch.
The Z disc anchors thin filaments; it does not bind the calcium that starts contraction.

why.correct: Leaking release channels keep calcium high, so troponin stays on and the muscles stay contracted. The calcium pumps work nonstop to clear calcium and the myosin heads keep splitting ATP. All that ATP use releases heat, so body temperature climbs.
options: The problem is in the SR release channel, not at the neuromuscular junction.
Correct. Uncontrolled calcium release drives both the rigidity and the heat.
The pumps keep working hard and using ATP; that is part of where the heat comes from.
The electrical steps are normal; the defect is in the channel the voltage sensor opens.

why.correct: The SR calcium ATPase, the myosin heads and the sodium–potassium pump all split ATP. Calcium flowing out of the SR and acetylcholine diffusing across the cleft both move down their gradients and need no ATP.
options: Correct. The SR calcium pumps are ATPases working against a steep gradient.
Release is passive: calcium flows down its gradient through open channels.
Correct. Myosin heads split ATP for the energy of each pull; the next topic shows how.
Diffusion needs no ATP.
Correct. The sodium–potassium pump restores the gradients over time.

why.correct: The action potential can only reach the voltage sensors at the triads by traveling down the T tubules. Cut off from the surface, the tubules stay at rest, the ryanodine receptors stay closed and little calcium is released, so the fiber barely contracts.
options: A surface action potential alone cannot open the SR release channels, which sit at the triads inside the fiber.
Skeletal muscle does not rely on calcium entering from outside, so no extra calcium arrives this way.
The pumps are in the SR membrane and are unaffected; the problem is that little calcium is released.
Correct. Without T tubules, excitation and contraction are uncoupled.

why.correct: Relaxation requires the sarcoplasmic calcium to fall, and that means pumping it back into the SR against a gradient of thousands to one, using ATP. (The myosin heads also need ATP to let go of actin.)
options: Muscle can only pull. Elastic proteins, opposing muscles and gravity lengthen it.
There are no inhibitory signals to skeletal muscle; the motor neuron simply stops firing.
Correct. Calcium ATPases use ATP to clear the sarcoplasm.
Acetylcholine is split by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft; only its choline is taken back.

why.correct: E-C coupling is the sequence that connects the electrical event (the muscle fiber action potential) to the mechanical one (contraction), with calcium release as the link.

Correct. It couples excitation to contraction.
Skeletal muscle fibers are not joined by gap junctions; each is excited by its own junction.
Myosin binding actin is the result of E-C coupling, its last step, not the whole sequence.

why.correct: The SR releases only part of its store with each action potential, and the pumps have not yet cleared the first pulse. The second release adds to what is left, so calcium climbs higher. A later topic shows how this lets the nervous system grade force.

The pumps run continuously, but the second release adds calcium faster than they can remove it.
One action potential releases only part of the SR store, and at 15 ms the refractory period is over. The second action potential fires and releases more calcium, so the level cannot hold steady.
Calcium in the sarcoplasm does not fall to zero, and here a new release is adding calcium rather than removing it.

why.correct: A skeletal muscle fiber's action potential is brief, about 2 to 5 ms, much shorter than the contraction it triggers.
options: That is the length of a heart muscle cell's action potential, not a skeletal fiber's.
Correct. It is over long before force peaks.
That is far longer than any single action potential in skeletal muscle.
That is roughly how long force lasts after one action potential, not the action potential itself.

why.correct: The A band is the length of the thick filaments, and the thick filaments do not change length. The thin filaments slide in over them, so the A band keeps its width while everything defined by a gap narrows.
options: The I bands are clearly narrower in the contracted sarcomere, because thick filaments now reach farther toward the Z discs.
The H zone has almost vanished, because the thin filaments from both ends now nearly meet.
Correct. The A band, the thick filaments' length, is unchanged.
The Z discs are closer together; that is the shortening of the sarcomere.

why.correct: The cocked head binds actin, forming a cross-bridge. Releasing phosphate drives the power stroke, and ADP leaves at its end, leaving the head tightly bound. A new ATP binding makes it let go, and splitting that ATP recocks it for the next turn.

Without ATP, the cross-bridge cycle stops after the power stroke. Heads that bind actin cannot let go, the calcium pumps fail so the binding sites stay uncovered, and the locked filaments make the muscles stiff: rigor mortis.

variables.name: Myosin heads detaching from actin
variables.why: A head lets go of actin only when a new ATP binds it; with no ATP, attached heads stay attached.

variables.name: Number of cross-bridges attached
variables.why: Calcium leaking into the sarcoplasm uncovers actin, heads bind and complete their stroke, and none can detach.

variables.name: Stiffness of the muscle
variables.why: Locked cross-bridges bolt the thick and thin filaments together, so the muscle cannot be stretched.

variables.name: Calcium pumped into the SR
variables.why: The SR calcium pumps are ATPases; without ATP they stop.

why.correct: Binding ATP is what releases a head from actin, so the heads detach. But splitting ATP is what recocks them. A head already cocked from an earlier split can make one stroke at most. After that it never returns to the high-energy position needed to bind and pull. No sustained force develops, and the muscle stays slack.
options: Correct. Detachment works; recocking does not.
Rigor needs heads stuck on actin with no ATP bound. Here ATP binds, so the heads come off.
The power stroke uses energy stored in the cocked head from an earlier split. Each head can spend that store once at most. Binding ATP releases the head but cannot recock it.
The drug acts on myosin, not on the SR calcium pumps, so calcium is still cleared after stimulation.

why.correct: The I band is the part of the sarcomere not covered by thick filaments: 2.2 − 1.6 = 0.6 µm, split as 0.3 µm on each side of the sarcomere.
