Correct. Sarcomere length minus A band: 2.2 − 1.6 = 0.6 µm.
This adds the two lengths instead of subtracting; the I band must be shorter than the sarcomere.
This comes from subtracting two thin filament lengths (2 × 1.0 µm), which gives the H zone if the thin filaments are 1.0 µm long, not the I band.

why.correct: The H zone is the part of the sarcomere the thin filaments from the two ends do not reach: sarcomere length − 2 × 1.0 µm. Before: 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 µm. After: 2.1 − 2.0 = 0.1 µm.
options: The H zone depends on how far the thin filaments slide in, so it changes as the sarcomere shortens.
This reverses before and after; more overlap makes the H zone narrower, not wider.
These values subtract only one thin filament length, but thin filaments reach in from both ends.
Correct. 0.4 µm narrows to 0.1 µm as the thin filaments slide toward each other.

why.correct: After death, ATP runs out. Calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm and uncovers actin, heads bind and complete their stroke, and without ATP to bind them they cannot let go. The locked cross-bridges hold the filaments together: rigor mortis.
options: Nerves and muscle membranes stop firing after death; the stiffness is in the filaments, not the membranes.
Correct. Rigor is locked cross-bridges.
Acetylcholine acts only on the end plate's channels; it does not hold filaments together.
Covered binding sites would leave the muscle relaxed and easy to stretch, the opposite of rigor.

why.correct: Binding of a fresh ATP changes the head's shape so it no longer grips actin. Splitting the ATP comes afterward and recocks the head.
options: Phosphate release goes with the power stroke, while the head is still attached.
Calcium leaving troponin stops new heads from binding, but a head already attached still needs ATP to let go.
Correct. ATP binding releases the head.
Splitting ATP recocks a head that has already let go.

why.correct: Thin filaments slide toward the M line, so overlap increases, the Z discs are pulled closer, and the I bands and H zone, which are gaps between filaments, narrow. The A band and the filaments themselves keep their lengths.
options: Correct. The thin filaments are anchored to the Z discs and pull them inward.
Correct. The thick filaments now reach closer to the Z discs.
The A band is the length of the thick filaments, which does not change.
Correct. The thin filaments from both ends move toward each other.
Filaments slide; neither kind shortens.
Correct. Sliding increases the overlap.

why.correct: It is the binding of a new ATP, not its splitting, that makes the head let go. Splitting happens after detachment and recocks the head.
options: This step is right. The cocked head binds an uncovered site, forming a cross-bridge.
This step is right. This is the power stroke.
This step is right. After ADP leaves, the head is tightly bound until ATP arrives.
This is the error. ATP binding, not splitting, detaches the head.
This step is right. Hydrolysis energy resets the head to its high-energy position.

why.correct: A cross-bridge is a myosin head bound to actin. It exists only while the head is attached.
options: A Z disc anchors thin filaments at the ends of a sarcomere.
Correct. The head bridges across to the thin filament.
A triad is a T tubule with two terminal cisternae.
The power stroke is the pivot a cross-bridge makes, not the attached head itself.

why.correct: The A band spans the thick filaments from end to end. If the thick filaments shortened, the A band would narrow. Because it stays the same while the I band shrinks, the thin filaments must be sliding in over thick filaments of constant length.
options: The A band is set by the thick filaments; the thin filaments reach into it from the ends.
The I band contains thin filaments only.
Correct. A constant A band means constant thick filaments.
Some proteins do change shape; the evidence here comes from the bands, not from a rule about proteins.

why.correct: The heads on each half of a thick filament point away from the M line, mirror images of each other. Every power stroke pulls a thin filament toward the M line, so the two sets of thin filaments, and the Z discs they are anchored to, move inward from both ends.
options: Correct. The mirror-image arrangement of the heads sets the direction.
The Z discs are pulled by the thin filaments; they do not pull on their own.
Calcium is released from terminal cisternae at the triads and spreads through the whole sarcomere.
Thin filaments on both sides are built from the same actin, troponin and tropomyosin.

why.correct: Splitting ATP recocks the head into a bent, high-energy position, like setting a mousetrap. The power stroke releases that stored energy as movement, after the head binds actin and lets go of its phosphate.
options: Binding actin triggers the stroke, but the energy was stored in the head's shape before it bound.
Calcium acts as a switch that uncovers the binding sites; it does not supply energy for the stroke.
A new ATP binds after the stroke and releases the head; its energy is used for the next recocking.
Correct. The energy is stored in the cocked head.

why.correct: Two conditions keep the cycle running: calcium on troponin and ATP. With calcium kept high and ATP present, the heads keep cycling and the fiber stays contracted. That is a sustained contraction, not rigor, because every head can still let go.

variables.name: Binding sites on actin left uncovered
variables.why: With calcium staying on troponin, tropomyosin stays off the binding sites.

variables.name: Cross-bridge cycling
variables.why: ATP is available, so heads keep binding, pulling, detaching and recocking for as long as the sites are uncovered.

variables.name: Time the fiber stays contracted
variables.why: Relaxation needs calcium to leave troponin, and the pumps that would lower it are blocked.

variables.name: Number of heads locked on actin as in rigor
variables.why: Rigor needs a lack of ATP. Here ATP binds and releases each head, so the heads keep cycling rather than locking.

why.correct: Rigor passes off over one to three days as enzymes released inside the dead fibers break down the muscle proteins. The locked cross-bridges are not released; the structure they hold together falls apart.
options: The pumps need ATP, and there is none; calcium does not return to the SR after death.
Letting go requires ATP to bind, and recocking requires ATP to be split; neither is available.
Correct. Protein breakdown, not cross-bridge release, ends rigor.
Anaerobic breakdown of glycogen stops within hours of death, before rigor is even complete.

why.correct: Sarcomeres in series add their shortening: 20,000 × 0.4 µm = 8,000 µm. Since 1 cm = 10,000 µm, that is 0.8 cm.
options: Correct. 8,000 µm = 0.8 cm.
This treats 1 cm as 1,000 µm; 1 cm is 10,000 µm.
Every sarcomere shortens by 0.4 µm, and in series their shortenings add; the whole myofibril shortens far more.
This treats 1 cm as 100,000 µm; 1 cm is 10,000 µm.

why.correct: In the power stroke, a myosin head bound to actin releases its phosphate and pivots at its hinge, dragging the thin filament a few nanometers toward the M line.
options: ATP binding is the detachment step that follows the stroke.
Correct. The pivot of the attached head is the power stroke.
Calcium release is part of excitation–contraction coupling, which allows the cycle to start.
The action potential is the electrical signal that starts the whole sequence, not a movement of myosin.

why.correct: A motor unit is one motor neuron together with every muscle fiber its axon branches reach. One action potential in that neuron makes all of those fibers contract.
options: It is the other way round. Each skeletal muscle fiber has one neuromuscular junction and answers to one motor neuron; one neuron supplies many fibers.
Correct. One neuron plus all of its fibers.
That is a fascicle, an anatomical bundle. A motor unit's fibers are scattered through the muscle and do not match fascicle boundaries.
That describes a single neuromuscular junction, one contact point between a neuron and one fiber, not the whole unit.

why.correct: Each extra motor unit adds its fibers' force all at once. When a unit has only 10 to 20 fibers, each step in force is tiny, so the eye can be turned by very small, precise amounts.
options: Small motor units give fine control, not great force. The calf, with large units and many more fibers, produces far more force.
Motor unit size says nothing about relaxing; every twitch still ends with calcium being pumped back into the SR.
Correct. Small units mean small steps of force, which allows fine control.
Every skeletal muscle fiber, eye muscles included, contracts only when its motor neuron fires.

why.correct: This is the latent period. The action potential travels along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules, the SR releases calcium, and calcium binds troponin. Cross-bridges are only starting to form and take up slack, so no tension shows yet.
options: Correct. Excitation–contraction coupling is under way; tension just has not risen yet.
One stimulus is enough to produce a full twitch. The fiber is busy with excitation–contraction coupling, not waiting.
Calcium is pumped back during the relaxation period, at the end of the twitch, not at the start.
ATP does not run out in a single twitch, and detaching cross-bridges would lower tension that had already risen.

why.correct: Tension falls only as calcium is cleared from the cytosol and tropomyosin covers the binding sites again. The SR's calcium pump moves calcium against its gradient and takes longer than the burst of release, so relaxation is the slow part of a twitch.
options: A twitch is the response to one action potential. If the neuron kept firing, the result would be summation, not a slow relaxation.
Tension falls as the tendon and connective tissue recoil, not as they are stretched. The stretching happens while tension rises.
Acetylcholinesterase breaks acetylcholine down within milliseconds, long before the twitch ends.
Correct. Relaxation waits on the calcium pump, which is slower than release.

why.correct: Both traces come from repeated stimuli. On the left, each stimulus arrives before the fiber has relaxed, so twitches sum in waves. On the right, stimuli arrive so fast that there is no time to relax at all, and the waves fuse into complete tetanus.
options: A fiber's twitch is all-or-none: once a shock reaches threshold, a stronger shock does not make that fiber contract harder. Frequency, not strength, changes the pattern.
Correct. Higher frequency turns wave summation into complete tetanus.
The traces show how one set of fibers responds over time. Fewer motor units would lower tension, not smooth out the waves.
One action potential gives one twitch however long the shock lasts. A sustained contraction needs repeated action potentials.

why.correct: Raising the frequency shortens the gap between action potentials until calcium can no longer be cleared between them. Calcium stays high, the fiber stops relaxing, and tension sums from separate twitches to complete tetanus, several times a single twitch's tension.

variables.name: Time between action potentials
variables.why: At 80 per second, a new action potential arrives every 12.5 ms instead of every 500 ms.

variables.name: Calcium released by each action potential
variables.why: Each action potential is all-or-none and releases about the same pulse of calcium from the SR; what changes is how often the pulses come.

variables.name: Average calcium level in the cytosol
variables.why: Calcium is released again before the pumps have cleared the last release, so it stays high.

variables.name: Relaxation between contractions
variables.why: There is no time to pump calcium back between stimuli, so the fiber cannot relax.

variables.name: Peak tension
variables.why: Sustained high calcium keeps cross-bridges cycling long enough to pull the elastic parts fully taut, so the twitches sum toward complete tetanus.

why.correct: The latent period covers the first three steps: the motor neuron signal, the fiber's action potential down the T tubules and the release of calcium onto troponin. Tension rises only when cross-bridges cycle (the contraction phase) and falls as calcium is pumped back (the relaxation phase).

A skeletal fiber's action potential and refractory period last a few milliseconds, but its twitch lasts tens of milliseconds. So new action potentials, each releasing more calcium, can fire while the fiber is still contracting, and the twitches sum.
options: Correct. A short refractory period lets new action potentials fire during the twitch.
Acetylcholine is released only when an action potential reaches the terminal, and acetylcholinesterase clears it fast. Each release triggers one fiber action potential.
The SR does have a calcium pump; it is what ends each twitch. Tetanus happens because release outpaces pumping.
Skeletal muscle fibers are not joined by gap junctions; each fiber is excited by its own neuromuscular junction.

why.correct: Force is graded by recruitment (more units, with larger ones joining as force rises) and by firing rate (moving units from summation toward tetanus). A single fiber's action potential and twitch are all-or-none, so the nervous system cannot make an individual fiber contract harder by a stronger signal.
options: Correct. More motor units means more fibers pulling.
Correct. Faster firing makes twitches sum toward tetanus.
Action potentials are all-or-none; a fiber's action potential is the same size whenever it fires.
Correct. By the size principle, larger units join as the required force grows.
A fiber's response to one action potential is fixed; extra force comes from more fibers and faster firing, not a bigger twitch.

why.correct: Small motor neurons reach threshold with less synaptic input, so they fire first. Larger ones join only as input grows. This size principle gives fine steps of force at low effort and big steps at high effort.
options: The largest motor neurons need the most input to reach threshold, so they join last, not first.
Force rises by adding units one after another; firing all of them at once would give a large jump in force even for a light grip.
Recruitment order is orderly and repeatable, set by motor neuron size.
Correct. This is the size principle.

why.correct: Her muscles develop tension that matches the load (her body weight), so their length and the joint angles stay the same. Tension without a change in length is an isometric contraction.
options: In a concentric contraction the muscle shortens and a joint moves. Her trunk stays still.
In an eccentric contraction the muscle lengthens under load. Her muscle length is not changing.
Correct. Tension rises, length stays the same.
A twitch lasts about a tenth of a second. A 45-second hold needs many motor units firing repeatedly, in summation and tetanus.

why.correct: The weight of the box is greater than the tension in the muscle, so the muscle is pulled longer. Its cross-bridges keep working to resist, which controls the speed. This is an eccentric contraction.
options: If the muscle relaxed completely, the box would drop, not descend slowly. Controlled lowering needs active tension.
Correct. Active tension while the muscle lengthens is an eccentric contraction.
Gravity pulls the box down; the muscle that bends the elbow would shorten only if the box were being lifted.
The elbow angle is changing, so the muscle's length is changing. An isometric contraction would hold the box still.

why.correct: Once tension exceeds the load, the muscle that lifts the dumbbell shortens: a concentric contraction. It lengthens only when lowering a load, in an eccentric contraction.
options: This step is right. Recruited motor units supply the tension.
This step is right. Every lift begins isometrically, until tension matches the load.
This step is right. Only when tension exceeds the load does the dumbbell move.
This is the error. Lifting is a concentric contraction, so the muscle shortens.

why.correct: At 160 percent the line is near the bottom of its falling slope. The thin filaments have been pulled almost off the thick filaments, so few myosin heads can reach actin and few cross-bridges form.
options: Active tension depends on filament overlap, not on how far the fiber is stretched. Past the middle range, more stretch means less overlap and less tension.
Correct. Little overlap means few cross-bridges and little tension.
Thick filaments hit the Z discs when the sarcomere is too short, not too long. At 160 percent a little overlap remains.
The graph shows tension changing strongly with length. That is the length–tension relationship.

why.correct: When a sarcomere is very short, the thin filaments from each end crowd past each other in the middle and get in each other's way, and the thick filaments butt against the Z discs. Fewer cross-bridges can pull usefully, so tension falls.
options: Losing overlap is the problem at very long lengths, not short ones. When short, the filaments overlap too much.
Calcium release does not depend on how long the sarcomeres are in this way. The limit is mechanical.
ATP supply is not set by sarcomere length. A rested fiber at any length has ATP available.
Correct. Crowding in the middle and thick filaments against the Z discs limit tension.

why.correct: Low resistance to passive movement and a floppy posture mean reduced muscle tone: hypotonia.
options: Hypertonia is increased tone: the limb would feel stiff and resist being moved.
Complete tetanus is a sustained, fused contraction, the opposite of a floppy limb.
Correct. Hypo- means under: low tone.
Treppe is the staircase rise in twitch strength in a rested muscle; it does not describe resting tone.

why.correct: A twitch has three phases: the latent period (no tension yet), the contraction phase (tension rises) and the relaxation phase (tension falls).
options: Correct. Tension rises in the contraction phase.
The refractory period belongs to the action potential, and it is over within a few milliseconds, early in the twitch.
Complete tetanus is a fused contraction from many stimuli, not a phase of one twitch.
Recruitment is adding motor units to raise force; it is not a phase of a single twitch.

why.correct: In a single twitch, calcium is cleared before the cross-bridges have finished stretching the fiber's elastic parts, so tension never reaches its full value. When action potentials arrive faster than calcium is cleared, calcium stays high, cross-bridges keep cycling and tension builds to its maximum.
options: Action potentials are all-or-none; they are the same size in a twitch and in tetanus.
A motor unit's fibers are fixed by the branches of its neuron. Adding fibers is recruitment of other units, not tetanus of one fiber.
Correct. Sustained calcium allows sustained cycling and full tension.
The power stroke is the same; what changes is how long cross-bridges keep cycling.

why.correct: Treppe (staircase) is the rise in twitch strength over the first several twitches of a rested muscle, with full relaxation between them.
options: In wave summation each twitch starts before the last has relaxed. Here each twitch relaxes fully.
Correct. A staircase of peaks with full relaxation between twitches is treppe.
In incomplete tetanus the fiber relaxes only partly between stimuli, giving a wavy plateau above baseline.
Recruitment adds motor units in a whole muscle. This trace shows a change in the twitches themselves.

why.correct: Physiological tetanus is a normal fused contraction from fast motor neuron firing. In the disease, a bacterial toxin blocks inhibitory neurons in the spinal cord, so motor neurons fire without restraint and muscles are driven into sustained, painful contraction.
options: The toxin acts on neurons in the spinal cord, not on the muscle fibers' calcium pumps.
Correct. The disease is a failure of the nervous system's brakes on motor neuron firing.
A single twitch always ends when calcium is pumped back. His sustained spasm comes from repeated firing.
Losing motor neurons would cause weakness and floppy muscles, not sustained spasm.

why.correct: Creatine kinase transfers the phosphate group of creatine phosphate to ADP in one step, giving creatine and ATP. At rest it runs the other way and rebuilds creatine phosphate.
options: That is glycolysis, a chain of ten enzyme reactions, not creatine kinase.
Correct. Creatine phosphate + ADP gives creatine + ATP.
That is the SR's calcium pump, which spends ATP rather than making it.
That is myoglobin, an oxygen-binding protein, not an enzyme.

why.correct: Stored ATP and creatine phosphate are right beside the myosin heads, and creatine kinase remakes ATP in one step, so they supply most of the ATP in the first seconds of an all-out effort.
options: Aerobic respiration is the slowest system to deliver ATP; in the first seconds of a sprint it supplies only a small share.
Glycolysis speeds up within seconds, but in the first 5 seconds creatine phosphate supplies more. And muscle glycolysis runs mainly on stored glycogen, not glucose from the blood.
Correct. Creatine phosphate dominates the first seconds.
Lactate is a fuel for steadier work later. At the start of a sprint, muscle is making lactate, not using it.

why.correct: Each creatine phosphate remakes one ATP, so the total available is 5 + 20 = 25 mmol. Time = 25 mmol ÷ 2.5 mmol per second = 10 seconds.
options: 2 seconds is how long the stored ATP alone would last (5 ÷ 2.5). Creatine phosphate adds much more.
8 seconds counts only the creatine phosphate (20 ÷ 2.5) and leaves out the stored ATP.
Correct. (5 + 20) ÷ 2.5 = 10 seconds.
62.5 comes from multiplying 25 by 2.5. Time is the amount divided by the rate.

why.correct: Anaerobic: 90 ÷ 2 = 45 glucose. Aerobic: 90 ÷ 30 = 3 glucose. Anaerobic glycolysis uses 15 times as much glucose for the same ATP, which is why hard efforts drain glycogen fast.
options: The two numbers are swapped. The route with the lower yield per glucose needs more glucose.
These come from multiplying 90 by the yields. Glucose needed is ATP needed divided by ATP per glucose.
These are not 90 divided by either yield; check the division.

why.correct: A one-minute all-out run spends creatine phosphate early and relies heavily on fast glycolysis, which burns glycogen and produces lactate. Aerobic respiration is climbing too. Through it all, ATP itself falls only modestly, because it is remade almost as fast as it is used.

variables.name: Rate of glycolysis
variables.why: Rising ADP and phosphate and falling creatine phosphate speed up the glycolytic enzymes, which supply ATP fast.

variables.name: Lactate production
variables.why: Glycolysis makes pyruvate faster than the mitochondria can take it in, so pyruvate is turned into lactate, regenerating NAD+.

variables.name: Creatine phosphate
variables.why: Creatine phosphate is spent in the first seconds to remake ATP and is not rebuilt until she rests.

variables.name: Muscle glycogen
variables.why: Glycolysis runs mainly on glycogen stored in the fibers, and it uses glucose wastefully, 2 ATP each.

variables.name: ATP concentration in the fibers
variables.why: It falls only modestly, to roughly three quarters of its resting level, far less than creatine phosphate, because the energy systems remake ATP almost as fast as it is spent.

why.correct: Lactate forms when pyruvate is produced faster than the mitochondria can use it, which happens at high work rates even when some oxygen is present. Turning pyruvate into lactate regenerates the NAD+ that keeps glycolysis running.
options: Correct. Lactate forms when glycolysis outpaces the mitochondria.
ATP in a working fiber falls only modestly. If it truly ran out, the fiber would lock in rigor.
Creatine kinase handles creatine phosphate and ADP. A different enzyme converts pyruvate to lactate.
Glycolysis in muscle runs mainly on stored glycogen, and making lactate requires glycolysis to be running fast, not starved of glucose.

why.correct: The energy systems overlap. At 30 seconds, creatine phosphate is largely spent, glycolysis supplies the largest share and aerobic respiration a growing one. No system switches off; only their shares change.
options: Creatine kinase keeps working as long as some creatine phosphate remains, and aerobic respiration runs from the start too.
Aerobic respiration is rising, but at 30 seconds of an all-out effort it supplies well under half of the ATP.
Stored ATP and creatine phosphate last only about 10 seconds of all-out work.
Correct. All three run; their shares shift over time.

why.correct: Myoglobin is a red, iron-containing oxygen-binding protein. Muscles that work for long periods on aerobic respiration, such as a chicken's legs, and those of diving mammals hold much more of it, which darkens them.
options: Glycogen is a colorless storage carbohydrate; it does not color muscle.
Creatine phosphate is a colorless small molecule.
Lactate is colorless, and it does not accumulate in resting muscle.
Correct. Myoglobin is the red pigment of muscle.

why.correct: Because myoglobin binds oxygen more tightly, oxygen moves from the blood onto myoglobin, and myoglobin gives it up only when oxygen in the fiber drops low, as at the start of exercise or during a strong contraction. It is a small reserve and a shuttle toward the mitochondria.
options: Correct. Tighter binding makes it a reserve released at low oxygen.
The store is small, enough for seconds of hard work. Mitochondria can still run short of oxygen in sustained hard exercise.
Tighter binding does the opposite: it helps draw oxygen from the blood into the fiber.
Myoglobin only holds oxygen. ATP made with oxygen is made in the mitochondria.

why.correct: A myosin head needs a fresh ATP to let go of actin. With no ATP, cross-bridges stay locked and the fiber becomes rigid, as in rigor mortis. Fatigue slows the cross-bridges and calcium release before ATP can fall that far.
options: The opposite happens. Relaxation needs ATP for the SR's calcium pump and for detaching the myosin heads.
Glycolysis needs ATP to start each glucose; with no ATP, it could not run at all.
Calcium release is triggered by action potentials, not by a lack of ATP. Without ATP the SR pump could not take calcium back, but the locked cross-bridges are the critical problem.
Correct. ATP is needed to release myosin from actin; without it, rigor.

why.correct: After about two hours of running, muscle glycogen can be nearly used up. Fatty acids alone cannot be burned fast enough to supply ATP at racing pace, so her pace drops sharply: "hitting the wall".
options: Creatine phosphate matters in the first seconds of hard effort. It was spent and rebuilt many times over the race; it does not suddenly run out at mile 20.
Correct. Glycogen depletion limits long endurance events.
Lactate is a fuel, not a poison, and in a steady marathon it stays fairly low.
ATP stays near three quarters of its resting level even in severe fatigue. If it truly ran out, her muscles would lock rigid.

why.correct: Blood lactate returns to resting levels within about an hour, so it cannot explain soreness two days later. Downhill walking is mostly eccentric work for the thigh muscles, which causes small injuries inside the fibers; the soreness comes from that damage and the repair that follows.
options: Lactate dissolves and is cleared or burned within about an hour; it does not crystallize in muscle.
Creatine phosphate is rebuilt within minutes of rest.
Correct. Delayed soreness comes from small muscle injuries, especially after eccentric work.
A small leak of muscle proteins can accompany the injury, but the soreness itself comes from the injury and repair, not from myoglobin.

why.correct: EPOC pays for restoring creatine phosphate and ATP, reloading oxygen onto myoglobin and in the blood, clearing lactate, and the raised costs of recovery: a warmer body, hormones released in exercise, breathing and circulation and tissue repair. It is not a reserve banked for later.
options: Correct. Aerobic respiration rebuilds the phosphate stores within minutes.
Correct. Myoglobin gave up its oxygen during the run.
The body does not bank extra oxygen beyond its normal stores; EPOC restores those stores and pays recovery costs.
Correct. Lactate is burned or converted to glucose in the liver.
Correct. Warmth speeds every reaction, and hormones raise metabolism for a while.

why.correct: Glycogen supplies glucose, glycolysis makes pyruvate, ATP and NADH, and when pyruvate outruns the mitochondria it is turned into lactate, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Lactate then leaves and is used as fuel elsewhere.
Creatine kinase needs no oxygen. It transfers the phosphate from creatine phosphate to ADP in a single step, which is why this system is the fastest.
options: This step is right. The reaction reverses at rest, rebuilding creatine phosphate from ATP.
This step is right. Splitting ATP in the cross-bridge cycle leaves ADP behind.
This is the error. The creatine phosphate system is anaerobic.
This step is right. Together with stored ATP it covers roughly the first 10 seconds of all-out work.

why.correct: The phosphate group moves from creatine phosphate onto ADP, making ATP.
options: Correct. ADP plus a phosphate is ATP.
Lactate comes from pyruvate at the end of anaerobic glycolysis, not from creatine phosphate.
Pyruvate is the product of glycolysis.
Glucose is a fuel broken down in glycolysis; creatine kinase does not make it.

why.correct: Crushed muscle fibers break down and release myoglobin into the blood. It is small enough to be filtered by the kidneys, its red-brown color darkens the urine, and it can damage the kidneys, which is why crush victims get plenty of fluid.
options: Actin is a large filament protein; it does not color the urine.
Correct. Myoglobin is the red pigment released from damaged muscle.
Creatine kinase also leaks from damaged fibers and is measured in blood tests, but it is colorless and does not darken urine.
Troponin leaks from damaged muscle too, but in tiny amounts, and it is colorless.

why.correct: In steady exercise lasting more than a few minutes, over 95 percent of the ATP comes from aerobic respiration. At a comfortable intensity, fatty acids supply much of the fuel, with glucose and glycogen supplying the rest.
options: Correct. Steady, moderate work runs on aerobic respiration.
Glycolysis runs, but at a comfortable pace its pyruvate goes on into the mitochondria. Anaerobic glycolysis dominates only in hard efforts of up to a couple of minutes.
Creatine phosphate smooths out each contraction's demand, but it must itself be rebuilt with ATP from aerobic respiration; it is not the original source.
Stored ATP would last only a couple of seconds of hard work.

why.correct: Breaking down creatine phosphate and ATP releases inorganic phosphate. It weakens each cross-bridge's pull and reduces calcium release from the SR, and it is one of the best-supported causes of fatigue in hard, repeated contractions.
options: Lactate is a fuel, and adding it to rested muscle does not weaken it.
ATP stays near three quarters of its resting level even in severe fatigue.
Correct. Phosphate buildup is a leading cause of peripheral fatigue.
Myoglobin keeps its iron; it may give up its oxygen, but that does not destroy it.

why.correct: Immediately after the sprint, creatine phosphate and myoglobin oxygen are low and lactate is high. During recovery, extra oxygen (EPOC) powers aerobic respiration that rebuilds creatine phosphate, reloads myoglobin and clears lactate, and oxygen use drifts back toward resting.

variables.name: Oxygen use
variables.why: Oxygen use falls from its peak, but it stays above resting for several minutes (EPOC) while stores are rebuilt, so it declines gradually rather than dropping at once.

variables.name: Creatine phosphate in her leg muscles
variables.why: At rest, creatine kinase runs in reverse, using ATP from aerobic respiration to rebuild creatine phosphate; about half returns in 30 seconds.

variables.name: Oxygen bound to myoglobin
variables.why: Oxygen delivered by the blood reloads the myoglobin that gave up its oxygen during the sprint.

variables.name: Lactate in her leg muscles
variables.why: Lactate leaves the fibers into the blood, and heart, resting muscle and liver burn it or turn it into glucose; it is gone within about an hour.

why.correct: Slow oxidative (slow-twitch, type I) fibers have slow myosin and make their ATP by aerobic respiration, supported by many mitochondria, much myoglobin and many capillaries. They can work for hours.
options: Fast glycolytic fibers are fast, have few mitochondria and little myoglobin, and tire within a minute or two.
Fast oxidative fibers are rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, but they contract fast, not slowly.
Correct. Slow myosin plus aerobic metabolism.
Fiber types describe skeletal muscle. Smooth muscle is a different tissue.

why.correct: Elite distance runners' leg muscles are often 70 to 80 percent slow oxidative fibers, and training has given those fibers even more mitochondria, myoglobin and capillaries.
options: That describes a sprinter or thrower, whose events need brief, high power.
Correct. Endurance athletes have mostly slow oxidative fibers.
An elite marathoner's muscle is dominated by slow fibers, which are red, not pale.
Endurance training improves aerobic capacity with little growth in fiber size; thicker fibers come from resistance training.

why.correct: Total = 90 + 70 + 40 = 200. Only slow oxidative fibers are slow-twitch: 90 ÷ 200 = 0.45, or 45%.
options: 35% is 70 ÷ 200, the fast oxidative fibers, which are fast-twitch.
55% is the fast-twitch share: (70 + 40) ÷ 200.
80% adds slow oxidative and fast oxidative fibers ((90 + 70) ÷ 200). Fast oxidative fibers are fast-twitch.

why.correct: With few mitochondria and little myoglobin, fast glycolytic fibers make most of their ATP by anaerobic glycolysis and creatine phosphate. Their glycogen is used up fast and phosphate accumulates, so their force falls quickly.
options: Their myosin splits ATP very fast; that is what makes them fast fibers.
All skeletal fibers have an SR, and fast fibers have an especially well-developed one.
Correct. A glycolytic fiber spends its fuel quickly and builds up phosphate.
Fast glycolytic fibers belong to large motor units whose neurons fire at high rates when recruited.

why.correct: Oxidative fibers depend on oxygen arriving from capillaries around them. A small diameter keeps every mitochondrion close to the surface, so the diffusion distance for oxygen is short. A glycolytic fiber does not wait for oxygen, so it can be thick and hold many myofibrils.
options: Slow oxidative fibers actually have low glycogen stores; the glycogen-rich fibers are the thick, glycolytic ones.
Contraction speed depends on the myosin version and calcium handling, not on diameter. Slow oxidative fibers are thin and slow.
Correct. Short diffusion distance supports aerobic metabolism.
Slow oxidative fibers have the most myoglobin of all.

why.correct: At marathon pace, small motor units of slow oxidative fibers do most of the work aerobically. A sprint recruits the large, fast glycolytic units too, which make ATP fast by glycolysis, produce lactate and tire quickly, so the burst cannot last.

variables.name: Recruitment of fast glycolytic fibers
variables.why: By the size principle, the largest motor units, made of fast glycolytic fibers, join only when near-maximal force is needed.

variables.name: Rate of anaerobic glycolysis
variables.why: Fast glycolytic fibers make their ATP mainly by glycolysis, and every working fiber's ATP demand rises steeply.

variables.name: Lactate production
variables.why: Glycolysis makes pyruvate faster than the mitochondria can take it in, so pyruvate is converted to lactate.

variables.name: Share of ATP from aerobic respiration
variables.why: Aerobic respiration keeps running, but glycolysis now supplies a much larger share of the far greater total.

variables.name: How long she can keep this pace
variables.why: Fast glycolytic fibers fatigue within a minute or two as glycogen falls and phosphate builds up.

why.correct: Endurance training makes fibers better at aerobic respiration: more mitochondria, myoglobin and capillaries, and a shift of fast glycolytic fibers toward fast oxidative. The number of fibers does not change.

variables.name: Mitochondria per fiber
variables.why: Repeated aerobic work stimulates fibers to build more mitochondria and aerobic enzymes.

variables.name: Capillaries around each fiber
variables.why: Low oxygen and shear in working muscle release VEGF, which drives angiogenesis.

variables.name: Myoglobin content
variables.why: Oxidative fibers adapt to training by making more myoglobin.

variables.name: Proportion of fast glycolytic fibers
variables.why: Training shifts fast glycolytic fibers toward fast oxidative properties.

variables.name: Total number of fibers in the muscle
variables.why: Training changes what fibers are like, not how many there are; adult skeletal muscle adds few if any fibers.

why.correct: Endurance training improves aerobic capacity: angiogenesis adds capillaries, fibers build more mitochondria and myoglobin, and fast glycolytic fibers shift toward fast oxidative. Fiber number does not rise, and large increases in diameter come from resistance training.
options: Correct. Angiogenesis adds capillaries.
Correct. More mitochondria means more aerobic capacity.
Adult skeletal muscle fibers do not divide, and hyperplasia adds few if any fibers.
Correct. More myoglobin stores and shuttles more oxygen.
Endurance training causes little hypertrophy; thick fibers are a result of heavy resistance training.
Correct. The fast fibers become more oxidative.

why.correct: This is hypertrophy: existing fibers make more actin and myosin and add myofibrils, so each fiber's diameter grows. Muscle stem cells fuse with the fibers and add nuclei to support the extra protein.
options: Mature skeletal muscle fibers never divide, and hyperplasia adds few if any fibers in adult humans.
Correct. Hypertrophy of existing fibers.
Training builds muscle protein, not fat. Fat replacing fibers happens in diseases such as muscular dystrophy.
Tendons do not grow to hold new fibers; fiber number stays about the same.

why.correct: Growth by adding more cells is hyperplasia. In the pregnant uterus, smooth muscle cells mostly enlarge (hypertrophy), but some also divide (hyperplasia).
options: Hypertrophy is growth by enlargement of existing cells. It is the main change in the uterus too, but it does not add cells.
Atrophy is shrinking, the opposite of growth.
Angiogenesis is new capillary growth, which also happens in the pregnant uterus, but it is not growth by muscle cell division.
Correct. More cells means hyperplasia.

why.correct: Without use, the fibers broke down protein faster than they made it and lost myofibrils: disuse atrophy. The fibers and their motor neurons are still there, so with training they rebuild their myofibrils.
options: Correct. Disuse atrophy is reversible.
Muscular dystrophy is an inherited disease that affects many muscles; a cast does not cause it.
Disuse shrinks fibers but does not kill them. Scar replaces muscle after large injuries, not after immobilization.
The calf is thinner, not thicker, and the change is in the muscle.

why.correct: In a cast, motor neurons still fire and fibers still get some activity and nerve contact. With the nerve cut, the fibers receive no action potentials at all. They atrophy severely, and over months to years, without reinnervation, they are replaced by fat and connective tissue.
options: Loss of the nerve causes more atrophy, not less; lack of strain is not protective here.
Denervated muscle loses much more than muscle that keeps its motor neurons.
Skeletal muscle fibers contract only when their motor neuron fires; cut off, they cannot drive their own growth.
Correct. Denervation atrophy is severe and, without regrowth of the axons, permanent.

why.correct: Stem cells become myoblasts, which multiply and line up, then fuse into a multinucleated myotube. The myotube builds myofibrils, and as it matures its nuclei move to the edge, giving the adult fiber's many peripheral nuclei.

This is Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Without dystrophin, each contraction tears the sarcolemma, fibers die and leak creatine kinase, and repair gradually falls behind. Fat and connective tissue take the place of the lost fibers, so the calves look big while being weak.
options: Some fibers may enlarge early, but the bulk of the enlarged calf is not muscle; the boy is getting weaker, not stronger.
Correct. The large calves are fat and connective tissue, not muscle.
Hyperplasia adds few if any fibers in skeletal muscle, and the fibers here are dying.
Lactate is not stored in fibers; it leaves and is used as fuel within about an hour.

why.correct: During repeated training sessions, working fibers are low in oxygen and capillaries are sheared by fast flow. Fibers and capillary lining cells release VEGF, which makes endothelial cells of nearby capillaries divide and sprout into new capillaries.
options: Correct. VEGF drives new capillary sprouting.
Red blood cells do not build capillaries. New capillaries sprout from the endothelium of existing ones.
Muscle fibers do not become capillaries; new capillaries sprout from existing capillaries.
Losing the nerve causes atrophy, not new capillary growth.

why.correct: In sarcopenia, fast fibers shrink the most, so power, the ability to produce force quickly, falls even more than strength. Catching yourself after a trip needs fast, forceful contraction. Loss of motor neurons, leaving fewer but larger motor units, also coarsens control.
options: Aging does not convert slow fibers into fast ones; if anything, fast fibers are lost or shrink.
Mature skeletal muscle fibers never divide.
Myoglobin does not slow contraction; speed depends on the myosin and calcium handling.
Correct. Loss of fast-fiber size costs power, which a quick recovery step needs.

why.correct: Mature skeletal muscle fibers never divide. Repair comes from muscle stem cells, whose myoblast daughters fuse with the damaged fiber or with each other.
options: This step is right. Stem cells between the sarcolemma and the basal lamina start the repair.
This step is right. Some daughters become myoblasts and others return to rest, keeping the supply.
This is the error. Mature fibers do not divide.
This step is right. Fusion patches the fiber and adds nuclei.

why.correct: Slow oxidative fibers belong to the smallest motor units, which are recruited first, so gentle walking uses mainly them. A maximal jump recruits all motor units, from small to large, so all three types contract.
options: It is the reverse: low-force tasks use the small slow units, and a maximal effort adds the large fast ones.
Recruitment follows force. A slow walk needs only a small part of the muscle's units.
Correct. Small slow units first; large fast units join for maximal force.
Walking uses the calf muscles. And even in a jump, the small slow units fire first and stay active as the larger ones join.

why.correct: By the size principle, small motor units (slow oxidative fibers) are recruited first, then intermediate ones (fast oxidative), then the largest (fast glycolytic).
options: Smooth muscle is a different tissue, not part of a skeletal muscle's motor units.
Correct. The largest units, of fast glycolytic fibers, come last.
Firing rate does rise with force, but the next type recruited is fast glycolytic.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and has no motor units.

why.correct: The proportion of slow to fast fibers is strongly inherited and changes little with training in adults. Training changes what each fiber is like: the sprinter's fast fibers will be larger and more powerful, with shifts within the fast types.
options: Training shifts properties within the fast types but converts few fibers between slow and fast, so the proportions stay similar.
Correct. Inheritance sets the mix; training changes the fibers' size and properties.
Training clearly changes fiber size, mitochondria and capillaries, so the muscles will not be identical.
Adult skeletal muscle adds few if any fibers; growth is hypertrophy of existing ones.

why.correct: Smooth muscle has no troponin. Calcium binds calmodulin, and calcium–calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase.
options: Troponin is the calcium sensor in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Smooth muscle lacks it.
Correct. Calmodulin is smooth muscle's calcium sensor.
Myoglobin binds oxygen, not calcium.
Tropomyosin is present on smooth muscle thin filaments, but it does not bind calcium and is not the switch.

why.correct: Calcium enters through voltage-gated channels, binds calmodulin, and calcium–calmodulin switches on myosin light-chain kinase. The kinase phosphorylates the myosin heads, which can then bind actin and cycle.
Calcium–calmodulin binds and activates myosin light-chain kinase, the enzyme that phosphorylates the myosin heads.
options: Tropomyosin shifting off actin is the skeletal muscle switch, triggered by troponin. In smooth muscle the switch is on myosin.
Smooth muscle has no troponin.
Correct. MLCK is the enzyme calcium–calmodulin turns on.
Myosin phosphatase removes phosphate and causes relaxation; it is the opposite step.

why.correct: Smooth muscle has no troponin. In smooth muscle, calcium binds calmodulin in the cytosol, and the switch acts on myosin rather than on the thin filament.
options: This step is right. Much of smooth muscle's calcium enters from the extracellular fluid.
This is the error. Smooth muscle uses calmodulin, not troponin.
This step is right. Phosphorylation lets the myosin heads bind actin and cycle.
This step is right. Dense bodies anchor the thin filaments, so sliding pulls them together.

why.correct: Calcium still rises and still binds calmodulin, but calcium–calmodulin cannot switch on the blocked kinase. Myosin heads stay unphosphorylated and do not cycle, so the strip barely contracts.

variables.name: Calcium entering the fibers
variables.why: The drug acts after calcium entry; the calcium channels still open when the fibers depolarize.

variables.name: Calcium bound to calmodulin
variables.why: Calmodulin still binds the calcium that enters; the block is on the kinase that calcium–calmodulin activates.

variables.name: Phosphorylated myosin heads
variables.why: With the kinase blocked, no phosphate is moved onto the myosin heads.

variables.name: Force of contraction
variables.why: Unphosphorylated myosin heads cannot bind actin and cycle, so little force develops despite the calcium.

why.correct: When myosin heads are dephosphorylated while still attached to actin, they detach and reattach very slowly. These latch-bridges hold tension for hours at a small fraction of the ATP cost skeletal muscle would pay.
options: Rigor happens when there is no ATP at all. Latch-bridges do detach, only slowly, and the vessel can still relax.
Smooth muscle does have mitochondria; the saving comes from spending less ATP, not from making it differently.
Tetanus is a skeletal muscle response to rapid firing and costs a lot of ATP. Smooth muscle holds tension through the latch state.
Correct. Slowly cycling latch-bridges hold tension cheaply.

why.correct: Arterial smooth muscle depends heavily on calcium entering from the extracellular fluid. Blocking the channels lowers cytosolic calcium, less calcium–calmodulin forms, fewer myosin heads are phosphorylated, the muscle relaxes and the vessel widens.
options: Correct. Less calcium entry means less activation of the calmodulin switch.
Smooth muscle has no troponin.
Smooth muscle has no neuromuscular junctions; its nerve fibers release transmitter from swellings along their axons.
Blocking entry reduces the calcium available; it does not load extra into the SR, and relaxation comes from less calcium in the cytosol.

why.correct: Each increase in volume stretches the wall and raises tension briefly, then the smooth muscle slowly lets its tension fall back while staying at the new length. This stress-relaxation response keeps pressure low as the bladder fills.
options: Tetanus is a sustained skeletal muscle contraction; a contracting wall would raise pressure, not keep it low.
Correct. Stress-relaxation lets the wall accommodate each new volume.
Autorhythmicity describes cells that fire on their own; it would cause contractions, not a quiet fill.
Rigor means locked cross-bridges from a lack of ATP; it would stiffen the wall.

why.correct: Few gap junctions, contraction only when each fiber's own nerve endings fire, and little spontaneous activity are the marks of multi-unit smooth muscle.
options: Single-unit smooth muscle has many gap junctions, contracts as a sheet and is often spontaneous.
Correct. Nerve-by-nerve control of individual fibers is multi-unit.
Visceral smooth muscle is another name for single-unit smooth muscle.
Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart and is striated.

why.correct: Intestinal smooth muscle is single-unit. Pacesetter cells produce slow, spontaneous waves of depolarization, and gap junctions spread the resulting action potentials through the sheet, so it contracts as one unit without any input from the brain or spinal cord.
options: The loop has been cut off from the brain and spinal cord, and the fluid contains no motor neurons.
Random, independent contractions would not give regular, coordinated waves; the fibers are coupled.
Smooth muscle has no neuromuscular junctions, and the outside nerves have been cut.
Correct. Pacesetter rhythm plus gap junctions coordinates the sheet.

why.correct: Single-unit smooth muscle is a gap-junction-linked sheet with pacesetter activity that contracts when stretched, and it lines most hollow organs. Individual nerve control describes multi-unit smooth muscle, and no smooth muscle has sarcomeres.
options: Correct. Gap junctions let the sheet act as one unit.
Correct. Pacesetter cells set its rhythm.
This is multi-unit smooth muscle.
Correct. Stretch depolarizes the fibers and can trigger contraction.
Correct. These walls are mostly single-unit smooth muscle.
All smooth muscle is nonstriated; its filaments are not arranged in sarcomeres.

why.correct: Thin filaments anchor to dense bodies, and the filaments run at angles in a crisscross lattice. When cross-bridges pull, the dense bodies are drawn together along many diagonal lines, so the fiber shortens, widens and puckers.
options: Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres.
Correct. Diagonal pulls on the dense body network shorten and bunch the fiber.
Intermediate filaments link the dense bodies but do not contract; actin and myosin generate the force.
The fiber's volume stays about the same; it changes shape, it does not take in water.

why.correct: The zigzag junction where two cardiac muscle fibers meet end to end is an intercalated disc. It holds desmosomes and gap junctions.
options: Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiac fibers end to end.
Dense bodies are found in smooth muscle, where they anchor thin filaments.
Z discs lie inside each fiber, marking the ends of sarcomeres, not the junction between two fibers.
The sarcolemma is the membrane around a single fiber. The intercalated disc is where two fibers' membranes interlock.

why.correct: An action potential in a ventricular muscle fiber lasts about 250 to 300 ms, and the fiber cannot fire again until it has nearly relaxed. New action potentials cannot pile up during a contraction, so twitches cannot sum, and the heart relaxes and fills between beats.
options: Cardiac muscle does use troponin, as skeletal muscle does.
Cardiac fibers are linked by gap junctions in their intercalated discs; that spreads the beat, and it has nothing to do with preventing tetanus.
Correct. The long action potential blocks summation.
Cardiac muscle has an SR; it is smaller than skeletal muscle's but supplies most of the calcium.

why.correct: About 1 percent of cardiac fibers are specialized to drift to threshold on their own and fire repeatedly. Their action potentials spread through gap junctions to the rest of the heart, so it beats without any nerve input. Nerves only adjust the rate.
options: Stress-relaxation is smooth muscle's slow fall in tension after a stretch.
Correct. Autorhythmicity lets the heart set its own rhythm.
Cardiac muscle has no motor units; every fiber contracts every beat.
Latch-bridges are a smooth muscle mechanism for holding tension cheaply.

why.correct: Every cardiac fiber contracts with every beat, because gap junctions spread each action potential through the whole heart. Force is graded instead by how much calcium each beat releases (and by how far filling stretches the fibers), which sets how many cross-bridges form.
options: There are no resting fibers to recruit: all of them contract every beat.
The heart cannot sum beats into tetanus, because each action potential lasts nearly as long as the contraction.
Correct. More calcium per beat gives a stronger contraction.
Cardiac muscle is almost entirely aerobic and has little anaerobic capacity; switching fuel pathways does not make beats stronger.

why.correct: Cardiac muscle makes nearly all its ATP in its many mitochondria, which fill about a third of each fiber, and has little capacity for anaerobic glycolysis. Without oxygen from the blood, its ATP supply fails within about a minute.
options: Cardiac muscle is rich in myoglobin, but that small store lasts only seconds.
Correct. Dependence on aerobic respiration makes it vulnerable.
Cardiac muscle has more mitochondria than almost any other tissue.
Cardiac fibers are short and thin, and a capillary runs beside nearly every one.

why.correct: With myosin heads along the full length of each thick filament and no sarcomere walls to stop them, thin filaments can slide a long way while still overlapping heads, so smooth muscle keeps producing force as it shortens or stretches far.
options: Smooth muscle has no sarcomeres.
Smooth muscle has no Z discs; dense bodies anchor its thin filaments.
Correct. Heads along the whole thick filament allow long sliding.
Smooth muscle has no T tubules.

why.correct: In the latch state, calcium and kinase activity fall and myosin heads lose their phosphate while still attached. They cycle slowly, so tension is held at a small ATP cost.

variables.name: Rate of cross-bridge cycling
variables.why: Dephosphorylated heads that stay attached detach and reattach very slowly.

variables.name: ATP used per second
variables.why: Each cycle splits one ATP, so slower cycling uses far less ATP.

variables.name: Tension in the vessel wall
variables.why: The attached latch-bridges keep holding the thin filaments, so tension stays close to its level before the fall in calcium.

variables.name: Myosin light-chain kinase activity
variables.why: With less calcium, less calcium–calmodulin forms, so less of the kinase is active.

why.correct: Skeletal and cardiac muscle both use troponin as their calcium sensor on the thin filament. Smooth muscle has no troponin; it uses calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase, so it would be unaffected.
options: Smooth muscle is the one type that does not use troponin.
Smooth muscle lacks troponin, so it would keep working.
Smooth muscle lacks troponin; cardiac muscle would be affected.
Correct. Both striated muscle types rely on troponin.
